notes.4: Most candidates were able to deal successfully with the differentiation, with respect to t, of the parametric equations, and then go on to find successfully the equation of the tangent. It was evident that many candidates did not read the question thoroughly and did not give their correct, but unsimplified, equation in the required form involving integers. Some candidates erroneously equated to zero and went on to find a value for t, having misunderstood the demands of the question. It is important that the question is read carefully before ‘habit’ takes over and errors are made. Solution: 2x−y +4=0
notes.5: This question proved to be the most problematic question on the paper, with many candidates failing to score any meaningful marks. There were many misuses of the logarithmic values, for example, incorrect statements such as ln1.87=lnK +ln1.35pln2, which showed a complete misunderstanding of the question and thus made the awarding of marks difficult. This is clearly a topic of the syllabus which candidates need to work on. Solution: p=1.40, K =1.75
notes.6i: Most candidates were able to find the value of a correctly, usually by using the factor theorem, but on occasion by algebraic long division. Candidates who made use of algebraic long division were much more likely to make an error in the calculation of the value of a. Use of the factor theorem should be promoted above the use of algebraic long division when possible.

notes.8i: Many candidates misread the question and tried to rearrange the given equation into the form stated without any attempt at differentiation first and then rearrangement. Careful reading of any question prior to starting work on it is of paramount importance. For the candidates who did realise that differentiation needed to be done first, most were able to do so correctly using the product rule, but then had problems in using trigonometric identities and attempting to rearrange their often correct result into the required form.
notes.key_messages: Teachers should reinforce with all their candidates the need for full presentation of working, especially in questions where candidates are asked to prove a particular result. If necessary steps of working are omitted then full marks cannot be awarded. This applied particularly to Question 5 where often very good candidates failed to show sufficient working. Whilst Examiners will generally accept steps that can be done mentally or on a calculator, this does not apply to questions that require a rigorous proof. notes.general_comments: General comments While presentation of work for many candidates was satisfactory there were significant numbers of candidates whose work was untidy and difficult to follow. The rubric on the front of the Question Paper says ‘You are reminded of the need for clear presentation in your answers’. It is generally true that marks cannot be awarded if methods used are not clear. It is worth noting here a very common error: forgetting the ± sign. For example, in Question 8(ii), p² = 4  p = ±2.
